Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative unfolds primarily through a continuous, real-time scene—moving from the ferry dock, up the gravel path, and into the house—anchored by spare, tense dialogue and specific physical actions (securing the rope, dragging the suitcase, taking out the bread). Woven seamlessly into this scene are brief, well-placed moments of exposition and summary. Rather than halting the narrative for long backstory dumps, the writer uses details within the scene (Jonas losing his balance, the smell of old coffee, the rubber boots outside) to naturally trigger brief flashes of exposition about Henning's death and the estranged dynamic between Ilse and Jonas. This interplay keeps the pacing steady and the emotional tension engaging while providing all the necessary background information.
